Australia's natural disasters, in order.Cyclone Mahina: The deadliest cyclone in Australian history struck Bathurst Bay, Queensland, killing over 400, mostly pearl divers, and possibly raising a record storm surge.
Australia's natural disasters, in order.Black Friday bushfires: Fires on this day in Victoria killed 71 people. A Royal Commission afterward reshaped forest management and fire-fighting.
Australia's natural disasters, in order.Hobart's Black Tuesday fires: In a single day, fires around Hobart destroyed roughly 1,300 homes and killed 62. Many survivors had sheltered in the River Derwent.
Australia's natural disasters, in order.Cyclone Tracy: Cyclone Tracy hit Darwin on Christmas Eve and destroyed most of its buildings. It led Australia to rewrite its building codes.
Australia's natural disasters, in order.Ash Wednesday fires: Fires in Victoria and South Australia killed 75 people, whipped by dust-dry winds after a long drought. The day was a Wednesday in February.
Australia's natural disasters, in order.Newcastle earthquake: Australia's deadliest earthquake was only magnitude 5.6, but it killed 13 people and badly damaged the city's older masonry buildings.
Australia's natural disasters, in order.Thredbo landslide: A slope above the ski village collapsed, burying two lodges. Stuart Diver was pulled alive after about 65 hours under the rubble.
Australia's natural disasters, in order.Black Saturday fires: Australia's deadliest bushfire disaster killed 173 people, in extreme heat. It prompted new warning systems and the 'leave early' advice.
Australia's natural disasters, in order.Queensland floods: Floods covered an area in Queensland larger than France and Germany combined and swamped parts of Brisbane in January 2011.
Australia's natural disasters, in order.Black Summer fires: These fires burned more than 18 million hectares across Australia, and the smoke circled the globe before returning.

When these dance crazes took off.The Charleston: Named after Charleston, South Carolina and popularised by a 1923 Broadway show, it became the symbol of Jazz Age flappers.
When these dance crazes took off.Lindy Hop: Named after Lindbergh's 1927 transatlantic flight, it was danced at Harlem's Savoy Ballroom.
When these dance crazes took off.The Twist: Chubby Checker's 1960 hit was the first big craze with no partner contact, and it reached number one twice, in 1960 and 1962.
When these dance crazes took off.The Hustle: Van McCoy's disco song brought it to number one and made line-style partner dances a feature of discos.
When these dance crazes took off.The Moonwalk: Michael Jackson debuted it on the Motown 25 TV special in 1983, during 'Billie Jean'.
When these dance crazes took off.Vogue: Madonna's song popularised moves from Harlem's ballroom scene, later shown in the documentary Paris Is Burning.
When these dance crazes took off.Macarena: The song by Los del Río spent 14 weeks at number one in the US, and it was a stadium and wedding staple.
When these dance crazes took off.Cha Cha Slide: DJ Casper (Mr. C the Slide Man) created it for a Chicago gym instructor's workout, and it became a school dance staple.
When these dance crazes took off.Crank That (Soulja Boy): A teenage Soulja Boy posted the song and dance on early YouTube and MySpace before it reached number one.
When these dance crazes took off.The Floss: Teenager Russell 'Backpack Kid' Horning popularised it on SNL with Katy Perry, and the Fortnite emote spread it worldwide.

Game-changing inventions through history.The wheel: The earliest known wheels were potters' wheels in Mesopotamia; wheeled vehicles came centuries later.
Game-changing inventions through history.Paper: Traditionally credited to Cai Lun, a Han court official, though earlier fragments have been found.
Game-changing inventions through history.Gunpowder: Chinese alchemists seeking an elixir of immortality stumbled on it.
Game-changing inventions through history.Printing press: By 1500, presses in hundreds of towns had printed millions of books, quickly spreading ideas across Europe.
Game-changing inventions through history.Telescope: Dutch spectacle-maker Hans Lippershey applied for a patent in 1608; Galileo improved it the next year.
Game-changing inventions through history.Steam engine (Newcomen): Used to pump water from mines, it wasted fuel until Watt added a separate condenser.
Game-changing inventions through history.Electric battery: Alessandro Volta stacked zinc and copper discs to make his voltaic pile; the volt is named for him.
Game-changing inventions through history.Edison's light bulb: Edison tested thousands of filament materials, and Joseph Swan was developing a similar lamp in Britain.
Game-changing inventions through history.Airplane: The Wright brothers' first flight lasted 12 seconds and covered 120 feet.
Game-changing inventions through history.Penicillin: Fleming noticed mould killing bacteria on a neglected dish; mass production came during World War II.

Shakespeare plays, by when the story is.Troilus and Cressida: A bitter tragicomedy about the Trojan War that is hard to classify.
Shakespeare plays, by when the story is.Julius Caesar: Caesar is killed early on, and the play is really about Brutus; 'Et tu, Brute?' is not in Roman sources.
Shakespeare plays, by when the story is.Antony and Cleopatra: Based on Plutarch's Lives via North's translation, it ends with Cleopatra's death by asp.
Shakespeare plays, by when the story is.Macbeth: The real Macbeth ruled Scotland from 1040 to 1057 and seems to have been a decent king.
Shakespeare plays, by when the story is.King John: Magna Carta, the great event of this reign, is famously never mentioned in the play.
Shakespeare plays, by when the story is.Richard II: Essex's rebels paid to stage this one in 1601, hoping to stir up a revolt.
Shakespeare plays, by when the story is.Henry IV, Part 1: It introduces Falstaff, one of Shakespeare's greatest comic creations.
Shakespeare plays, by when the story is.Henry V: It features the battle of Agincourt and the 'band of brothers' speech.
Shakespeare plays, by when the story is.Richard III: The real king's skeleton was found beneath a Leicester car park in 2012.
Shakespeare plays, by when the story is.Henry VIII: During a 1613 performance a cannon set the Globe's thatch alight and the theatre burned down.

When these famous women died.Hatshepsut: Egypt's female pharaoh had her images later chiseled away by her successor.
When these famous women died.Sappho: The Greek poet from Lesbos survives only in fragments, plus one nearly complete poem.
When these famous women died.Cleopatra: Despite her fame she was Macedonian Greek by descent, and the first of her family to learn Egyptian.
When these famous women died.Boudica: She led the Iceni revolt against Rome, burning Londinium to the ground.
When these famous women died.Hypatia: The Alexandrian mathematician and philosopher was killed by a mob.
When these famous women died.Empress Theodora: She rose from entertainer to empress, co-ruling with Justinian.
When these famous women died.Wu Zetian: The only woman to rule China as emperor in her own right.
When these famous women died.Olga of Kyiv: She ruled as regent for her son, took brutal revenge on the Drevlians, and became a Christian saint.
When these famous women died.Eleanor of Aquitaine: Queen of France, then of England, she was mother of Richard the Lionheart and King John.
When these famous women died.Joan of Arc: Executed at about 19, she was declared a saint in 1920, after being cleared in a 1456 retrial.

Chess by the numbers.Kings per side: Each side has one king, and the entire game revolves around trapping the opponent's, which can never be captured.
Chess by the numbers.Black's move in Fool's Mate: Fool's Mate is the quickest possible checkmate, and it takes only two moves by Black, though White has to cooperate badly.
Chess by the numbers.Repetitions for a draw: Threefold repetition lets a player claim a draw, and it stops endless back-and-forth moves when neither can progress.
Chess by the numbers.Pawns per side: Pawns can become any piece except a king on reaching the far side, and they are the soul of chess, according to Philidor.
Chess by the numbers.Pieces per side: Each side starts with 16 pieces, and the total number of possible chess games is greater than the number of atoms in the universe.
Chess by the numbers.Legal first moves for White: White has 20 legal first moves, 16 by pawns and 4 by knights, and that number grows quickly.
Chess by the numbers.Squares a central queen hits: A queen in the center of an empty board attacks 27 squares, which is why it's the most powerful piece.
Chess by the numbers.Pieces at the start: The 32 pieces start on the board, and as the game goes on, they get traded off, until only a few remain.
Chess by the numbers.The no-capture draw rule: The fifty-move rule says a draw can be claimed if there has been no capture or pawn move in 50 moves.
Chess by the numbers.Squares on the board: The 64 squares of the board alternate light and dark, and the board is always set up with a light square in the right-hand corner.

Scoville heat, from salad to pure capsai.Cucumber: It contains no capsaicin at all, and it is about 95 percent water, which is why it cools the mouth.
Scoville heat, from salad to pure capsai.Pimento: It is the sweet red filling stuffed into green olives and mixed into pimento cheese.
Scoville heat, from salad to pure capsai.Anaheim pepper: It is named for Anaheim, California, although it originated in New Mexico.
Scoville heat, from salad to pure capsai.Chipotle: A smoked, dried jalapeno, its name comes from the Nahuatl for smoked chili.
Scoville heat, from salad to pure capsai.Tabasco pepper: Edmund McIlhenny used these peppers for the sauce, aged in barrels on Avery Island, Louisiana.
Scoville heat, from salad to pure capsai.Malagueta pepper: This chili is a staple in Brazilian cooking, especially in the dishes of Bahia.
Scoville heat, from salad to pure capsai.Scotch bonnet: Its shape resembles a Scottish tam, which gave rise to its name, and it is key to Jamaican jerk.
Scoville heat, from salad to pure capsai.Trinidad Moruga Scorpion: It was named hottest chili in 2012 by New Mexico State University.
Scoville heat, from salad to pure capsai.Pepper X: Created by Ed Currie, it was declared the world's hottest chili by Guinness in 2023, beating the Carolina Reaper.
Scoville heat, from salad to pure capsai.Pure capsaicin: Pharmacist Wilbur Scoville invented the scale in 1912, using human tasters; today machines measure it.

Roman numerals, by value.IV: IV is subtractive notation: a smaller numeral before a larger one means subtract, so 'one before five' is four, though clocks often show IIII.
Roman numerals, by value.IX: IX works the same way as IV, one before ten, and it appears on clock faces and in Super Bowl names such as Super Bowl IX.
Roman numerals, by value.XIV: XIV combines X and IV; the 14th Super Bowl and French king Louis XIV, the Sun King, both use it.
Roman numerals, by value.XL: XL, ten before fifty, gives forty, and you will see it in clothing as 'extra large', where it has nothing to do with Rome.
Roman numerals, by value.XC: XC is 'ten less than a hundred'; many Roman numerals work like this, and XC appears in film copyright dates in the 1990s.
Roman numerals, by value.CD: CD means 'a hundred less than five hundred', and it is also the abbreviation for compact disc, a coincidence in letters.
Roman numerals, by value.DC: DC is simply 500 plus 100; it is also the abbreviation for Washington, District of Columbia, and a comic-book publisher.
Roman numerals, by value.CM: CM is 'a hundred before a thousand', and the Romans themselves did not always use subtraction, writing 900 as DCCCC.
Roman numerals, by value.MCM: MCM is 1,000 plus 900, which is why movies and books of the 20th century carry copyright years starting MCM.
Roman numerals, by value.MMXX: MMXX is 2020; the double M is 2,000 plus XX. Rome had no zero, so the numeral system could not express it.

How long these epic poems are.Sir Gawain & the Green Knight: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight is a 14th-century Arthurian poem in which a Green Knight challenges the court to a beheading game.
How long these epic poems are.Beowulf: Beowulf is the longest surviving Old English poem, and its single manuscript survived a fire in 1731.
How long these epic poems are.Song of Roland: The Song of Roland is the oldest major work in French literature, and tells of a heroic rear-guard battle at Roncevaux.
How long these epic poems are.Aeneid: The Aeneid was written by Virgil, and it is said he wanted it burned on his deathbed because it was unfinished.
How long these epic poems are.Odyssey: The Odyssey follows Odysseus for ten years as he returns from the Trojan War, and its sequel stories include the Cyclops and the Sirens.
How long these epic poems are.Divine Comedy: Dante's Divine Comedy is written in a rhyme scheme called terza rima that he invented, and it features journeys through Hell, Purgatory and Paradise.
How long these epic poems are.Iliad: The Iliad covers only a few weeks of the Trojan War, and begins with the rage of Achilles.
How long these epic poems are.Ramayana: The Ramayana tells how Rama, a prince, rescues his wife Sita from the demon king Ravana, and is retold across South and Southeast Asia.
How long these epic poems are.Shahnameh: The Shahnameh was written by Ferdowsi over about 30 years, and is a national epic of Persia, with a famous tale of Rostam and Sohrab.
How long these epic poems are.Mahabharata: The Mahabharata is about ten times longer than the Iliad and Odyssey combined, and contains the Bhagavad Gita.

Chinese, Japanese and Taiwanese cities,.Harbin: It is famous for its yearly ice and snow festival, where giant ice buildings are lit up, and for its Russian-influenced architecture.
Chinese, Japanese and Taiwanese cities,.Sapporo: It hosted the 1972 Winter Olympics, the first held in Asia, and is known for its snow festival and miso ramen.
Chinese, Japanese and Taiwanese cities,.Beijing: It was the first city to host both Summer and Winter Olympics, in 2008 and 2022.
Chinese, Japanese and Taiwanese cities,.Sendai: Nicknamed the City of Trees, it was hit hard by the 2011 tsunami.
Chinese, Japanese and Taiwanese cities,.Tokyo: Greater Tokyo is the most populous metropolitan area in the world, with around 37 million people.
Chinese, Japanese and Taiwanese cities,.Osaka: Known as Japan's kitchen, its motto kuidaore means roughly to eat until you drop.
Chinese, Japanese and Taiwanese cities,.Shanghai: Its maglev train to the airport is the fastest commercial train in the world, reaching about 430 km/h.
Chinese, Japanese and Taiwanese cities,.Naha, Okinawa: This was the capital of the Ryukyu Kingdom, and karate was born on the island.
Chinese, Japanese and Taiwanese cities,.Taipei: Taipei 101 here was the world's tallest building from 2004 to 2010.
Chinese, Japanese and Taiwanese cities,.Hong Kong: Its name means fragrant harbor, and it was a British colony until 1997.

Wingspans of famous aircraft.Wright Flyer: Its first flight on December 17, 1903 covered about 37 meters, which is shorter than a modern jumbo jet's wingspan.
Wingspans of famous aircraft.Concorde: Friction with the air heated the airframe in supersonic flight so much that Concorde stretched by up to about 25 centimeters.
Wingspans of famous aircraft.Boeing 737-800: The 737 family is the best-selling jetliner line ever, with more than 10,000 built; its engines are flattened underneath to clear the low wing.
Wingspans of famous aircraft.B-52 Stratofortress: Entered service in the 1950s and is still flying; the Air Force plans to keep upgraded B-52s flying into the 2050s.
Wingspans of famous aircraft.Boeing 787-9: Its carbon-fiber wings flex dramatically in flight, with the tips bending upward by several meters.
Wingspans of famous aircraft.Boeing 747-8: The last and longest 747, the 747-8 is the longest passenger airliner ever built at about 76 meters. The final one was delivered in 2023.
Wingspans of famous aircraft.Airbus A380: The double-decker's wingspan was set to just fit the 80-meter box that airports use to size gates and taxiways.
Wingspans of famous aircraft.Antonov An-225 Mriya: Only one was ever finished. It once carried a Soviet space shuttle on its back and was destroyed in 2022 during the battle for Hostomel airport.
Wingspans of famous aircraft.Hughes H-4 Spruce Goose: Howard Hughes flew it once, in 1947, for about a mile just above the water. Despite its nickname it was built largely of birch, not spruce.
Wingspans of famous aircraft.Stratolaunch Roc: A twin-fuselage carrier built to launch rockets from altitude. It has the widest wingspan of any aircraft that has ever flown.

Milestones of the space age.Sputnik 1 launched: The beach-ball-sized satellite, about 58 centimeters across, beeped radio signals for roughly three weeks and began the space race.
Milestones of the space age.Gagarin orbits Earth: Yuri Gagarin's flight lasted 108 minutes. He ejected near the ground and parachuted down separately from his capsule.
Milestones of the space age.Apollo 11 Moon landing: Armstrong and Aldrin spent about 21 hours on the surface while Collins orbited alone above.
Milestones of the space age.Skylab launched: America's first space station. After it was abandoned, its orbit decayed and debris fell over Australia in 1979.
Milestones of the space age.First Space Shuttle flight: Columbia's first flight carried John Young and Robert Crippen, in the first orbiter built to be reused.
Milestones of the space age.Mir core module launched: The Soviet then Russian station was assembled in orbit and stayed crewed for about 15 years before it was deliberately brought down in 2001.
Milestones of the space age.Hubble launched: Its mirror was flawed, so early images were blurry, until shuttle astronauts installed corrective optics in 1993.
Milestones of the space age.First ISS module launched: Zarya was Russian-built but US-funded. The ISS has been continuously occupied since November 2000.
Milestones of the space age.Dragon reaches the ISS: It became the first private spacecraft to dock with the International Space Station.
Milestones of the space age.First Falcon 9 booster landing: In December 2015, an orbital-class rocket first stage landed upright at Cape Canaveral, opening the door to reuse.

Cycling's big races, by first edition.Liege-Bastogne-Liege: Known as La Doyenne, the old lady, it is the oldest of the classics, and its final climbs have decided many editions.
Cycling's big races, by first edition.Paris-Roubaix: Called the Hell of the North for its brutal cobblestone sectors, it ends in a velodrome where winners get a cobblestone trophy.
Cycling's big races, by first edition.Tour de France: Its 21 stages run over three weeks and finish on the Champs-Elysees in Paris, and it is the sport's most famous race.
Cycling's big races, by first edition.Il Lombardia: The Race of the Falling Leaves is run in autumn, and is the last of the five Monuments of the season.
Cycling's big races, by first edition.Milan-San Remo: At about 290 kilometers, it is the longest one-day classic, called La Primavera, and it usually ends with a sprint finish.
Cycling's big races, by first edition.Giro d'Italia: The leader wears the pink jersey, a nod to the pink pages of the sponsor newspaper, the Gazzetta dello Sport.
Cycling's big races, by first edition.Tour of Flanders: It is known as the Ronde and is a Flemish national event, with steep cobbled climbs like the Koppenberg.
Cycling's big races, by first edition.Pro road world champs: The winner wears the rainbow jersey for a year, a prize every professional rider hopes to earn.
Cycling's big races, by first edition.Vuelta a Espana: The third of the Grand Tours, where the overall leader wears red, was first held in 1935 and is Spain's biggest race.
Cycling's big races, by first edition.Tour Down Under: The first WorldTour race of the season, held in Adelaide in January, long before European races start.

Famous diets, by year they appeared.Banting's Letter on Corpulence: William Banting, an undertaker, lost weight by cutting carbs, and in South Africa 'banting' still means low-carb eating.
Famous diets, by year they appeared.Ketogenic diet for epilepsy: It was developed in the 1920s to treat children with epilepsy, long before it became a weight-loss craze.
Famous diets, by year they appeared.Weight Watchers: Jean Nidetch started it by hosting friends in her Queens living room.
Famous diets, by year they appeared.Atkins: Dr Robert Atkins's 'Diet Revolution' made low-carb eating a mainstream fad.
Famous diets, by year they appeared.Slim-Fast: These meal-replacement shakes promised weight loss by swapping meals.
Famous diets, by year they appeared.Jenny Craig: It began in Australia, and became a household name in the United States.
Famous diets, by year they appeared.The Zone: Barry Sears' plan balanced 40 percent carbohydrate, 30 percent protein and 30 percent fat.
Famous diets, by year they appeared.South Beach: Cardiologist Arthur Agatston created it, and it was named for Miami's beach district.
Famous diets, by year they appeared.Whole30: The month-long plan removes sugar, grains, dairy and legumes before reintroducing them.
Famous diets, by year they appeared.5:2 fasting: Popularized by Michael Mosley, it means eating normally five days and restricting calories on two.

Summer Olympics in cities that hosted ju.St. Louis: The 1904 Games were folded into the World's Fair and dragged on for months; one marathon runner rode part of the way in a car.
Summer Olympics in cities that hosted ju.Antwerp: The first Games after World War I excluded Germany and others, and the flag with five rings debuted here.
Summer Olympics in cities that hosted ju.Amsterdam: The first Games with a flame lit in a tower, and women competed in athletics for the first time.
Summer Olympics in cities that hosted ju.Berlin: Jesse Owens won four golds despite Nazi propaganda, and the first Olympic torch relay was run here.
Summer Olympics in cities that hosted ju.Helsinki: The Soviet Union made its Olympic debut here, and Emil Zátopek won the 5,000 m, 10,000 m and marathon.
Summer Olympics in cities that hosted ju.Melbourne: The first Games in the Southern Hemisphere also began the tradition of athletes mingling in the closing ceremony.
Summer Olympics in cities that hosted ju.Rome: Ethiopia's Abebe Bikila won the marathon barefoot, finishing by the Arch of Constantine.
Summer Olympics in cities that hosted ju.Mexico City: At 2,240 meters, the thin air helped Bob Beamon leap about 55 cm beyond the old long-jump record.
Summer Olympics in cities that hosted ju.Munich: The Games were marred by the massacre of 11 Israeli athletes, and Mark Spitz also won seven golds there.
Summer Olympics in cities that hosted ju.Montreal: Nadia Comaneci scored the first perfect 10 in gymnastics, and the stadium debt took about 30 years to pay off.

Famous national parks by founding year.Yellowstone: Congress created it in 1872 as the world's first national park, and it holds more than half the world's geysers.
Famous national parks by founding year.Royal National Park, Australia: The world's second national park, just south of Sydney, was at first simply called 'National Park' before getting its royal prefix in the 1950s.
Famous national parks by founding year.Banff: Canada's first national park grew out of hot springs discovered by railway workers in the 1880s.
Famous national parks by founding year.Yosemite: John Muir campaigned to protect it, and its granite monolith El Capitan draws climbers from around the world.
Famous national parks by founding year.Grand Canyon: The Colorado River carved the canyon, which exposes rock nearly two billion years old at its depths.
Famous national parks by founding year.Kruger: South Africa's flagship park covers roughly the area of Wales and is home to the Big Five.
Famous national parks by founding year.Plitvice Lakes: A chain of 16 terraced lakes linked by waterfalls in Croatia, whose waters shift between green and blue.
Famous national parks by founding year.Serengeti: The name comes from the Maasai word for 'endless plain', and its annual migration involves over a million wildebeest.
Famous national parks by founding year.Galápagos: Charles Darwin visited in 1835, and the islands' finches and tortoises later helped inspire his ideas on evolution.
Famous national parks by founding year.Great Barrier Reef Marine Park: The world's largest coral reef system stretches about 2,300 km along Queensland and can be seen from space.

Stanley Kubrick films by release.Paths of Glory: Kubrick's World War I film, starring Kirk Douglas, was banned in France for years. It's a harsh look at military justice, and a favorite of film fans.
Stanley Kubrick films by release.Spartacus: This Roman epic, starring Kirk Douglas, was one Kubrick famously disowned, since he did not control the script. Dalton Trumbo's credit helped end the Hollywood blacklist.
Stanley Kubrick films by release.Lolita: Adapted from Nabokov's novel with James Mason, the film was shot in England. Censorship pressure at the time made the story's central relationship hard to depict.
Stanley Kubrick films by release.Dr. Strangelove: Peter Sellers played three roles in this Cold War satire about nuclear war, which Kubrick first meant to make as a serious drama, and it is a comedy classic.
Stanley Kubrick films by release.2001: A Space Odyssey: Kubrick developed it with author Arthur C. Clarke, and its effects were so groundbreaking that the film won an Oscar for visual effects.
Stanley Kubrick films by release.A Clockwork Orange: Kubrick himself had it withdrawn in Britain in the early 1970s after copycat violence and threats, and it stayed unavailable there until after his death in 1999.
Stanley Kubrick films by release.Barry Lyndon: Famous for scenes shot by candlelight using special lenses made for NASA, this period drama won four Oscars, including for cinematography.
Stanley Kubrick films by release.The Shining: Based on Stephen King's novel, it was shot in a huge set at Elstree, and King disliked it. Its Overlook Hotel carpet and twin girls are iconic.
Stanley Kubrick films by release.Full Metal Jacket: The film about Marines in Vietnam was mostly shot in England, in a disused gasworks and with imported palm trees.
Stanley Kubrick films by release.Eyes Wide Shut: His last film, starring then-married Tom Cruise and Nicole Kidman, was completed just days before Kubrick died in 1999.

Milestones in flight.Montgolfier balloon: The Montgolfier brothers' hot-air balloon first carried a sheep, a duck and a rooster before people flew in it over Paris in 1783.
Milestones in flight.Garnerin's parachute jump: André Garnerin made the first parachute descent without a frame, and he leapt from a balloon over Paris.
Milestones in flight.Giffard's steam airship: Henri Giffard's powered airship traveled about 27 km, and it was driven by a steam engine.
Milestones in flight.Lilienthal's gliders: Otto Lilienthal made thousands of flights in hanging gliders, inspiring the Wright brothers before he died in a crash.
Milestones in flight.Wright Flyer: Orville Wright flew this plane for 12 seconds at Kitty Hawk, and it covered about 37 meters.
Milestones in flight.Blériot crosses the Channel: Louis Blériot won a prize from the Daily Mail for flying across the English Channel in about 37 minutes.
Milestones in flight.Lindbergh's solo Atlantic: Charles Lindbergh flew non-stop from New York to Paris in the Spirit of St. Louis, and it won him a $25,000 prize.
Milestones in flight.Sikorsky's helicopter: Igor Sikorsky's VS-300 lifted off, and it was the first practical single-rotor helicopter.
Milestones in flight.Comet jetliner first flight: The de Havilland jetliner was the first jet-powered airliner, but metal fatigue caused several early crashes.
Milestones in flight.Concorde first flight: This Anglo-French supersonic airliner could cross the Atlantic in about three and a half hours.

Traditional book sizes.Sexagesimo-quarto (64mo): Sixty-four-mo books are pocket-sized, folded from a big sheet into 64 leaves, and are tiny enough to hold in the palm.
Traditional book sizes.Vigesimo-quarto (24mo): These small volumes, folded 24 to a sheet, were popular for pocket editions of poetry and classics.
Traditional book sizes.Sextodecimo (16mo): Sextodecimo means the sheet is folded into 16 leaves, and it's a size used for many small books in the 1800s.
Traditional book sizes.Duodecimo (12mo): The 12-leaf fold was a standard for small novels and Bibles, and the name comes from Latin for twelve.
Traditional book sizes.Octavo: The most common book size, made by folding each sheet three times to make eight leaves.
Traditional book sizes.Quarto: Made by folding a sheet twice for four leaves, it was a size used by Shakespeare's early editions.
Traditional book sizes.Folio: A folio is a sheet folded just once, and Shakespeare's First Folio of 1623 is the most famous example.
Traditional book sizes.Elephant folio: Elephant folio books were so large that they needed a sturdy lectern or table, and they were used for prestige art and natural-history plates.
Traditional book sizes.Atlas folio: Atlas folio is named for the map books it was built to hold, and those books borrowed the name of the Titan Atlas.
Traditional book sizes.Double elephant folio: Audubon's Birds of America used this size, with pages big enough to show even a large heron life-size, and a copy has sold for over $11 million.

How many species? Round two.Hippos: There are two living hippo species, the common hippo and the pygmy hippo, and the hippo is related to whales.
How many species? Round two.Big cats (Panthera): Monaco is the most densely populated country, and its Grand Prix is run on the streets.
How many species? Round two.Great apes (incl. humans): Great apes include humans, chimpanzees, bonobos, gorillas and orangutans.
How many species? Round two.Deer: Deer include moose, reindeer and the tiny pudu, and antlers are shed and regrown every year.
How many species? Round two.Whales and dolphins: Amsterdam has more bikes than residents, and most of its canals were dug during the 17th century.
How many species? Round two.Turtles: Turtles have shells made of fused ribs, and the oldest species have been around for over 200 million years.
How many species? Round two.Cichlid fish: Cichlids include many species in African lakes, and some species evolved in just a few thousand years.
How many species? Round two.Frogs: Rome was already home to around a million people in ancient times, and Vatican City sits entirely within it.
How many species? Round two.Ants: Berlin has more bridges than Venice, and it's the largest city in Germany and the EU's most visited capital.
How many species? Round two.Bees: London was founded by the Romans as Londinium around AD 47, and it was Europe's largest city for much of the 1800s.

When these strange museums were founded.Kunstkamera (St Petersburg): Peter the Great founded this cabinet of curiosities, and it contains anatomical specimens and oddities.
When these strange museums were founded.Mütter Museum: This Philadelphia museum displays medical oddities, including a cast of the conjoined twins Chang and Eng's liver.
When these strange museums were founded.Meguro Parasitological Museum: This Tokyo museum is devoted to parasites, and it displays a tapeworm over eight meters long.
When these strange museums were founded.Sulabh Museum of Toilets: This museum in Delhi covers the history of the toilet, and it's run by a social service group.
When these strange museums were founded.Museum of Bad Art: This museum shows terrible paintings that someone loved enough to rescue, and it began in a Boston-area basement.
When these strange museums were founded.Icelandic Phallological Museum: This Reykjavík museum collects phallic specimens from Icelandic and other animals.
When these strange museums were founded.Instant Ramen Museum: This Japanese museum celebrates instant noodles and was founded in honor of Momofuku Ando.
When these strange museums were founded.Int'l Cryptozoology Museum: Cryptozoology is the study of hidden animals, and the museum in Portland, Maine is devoted to creatures like Bigfoot.
When these strange museums were founded.Museum of Broken Relationships: A museum in Zagreb exhibits objects from failed relationships, each with a personal story.
When these strange museums were founded.Museum of Failure: This traveling Swedish museum shows failed products and the lessons from them, and was founded by Samuel West.

Resting heart rate.Blue whale (diving): The heart can weigh around 180 kg, and beats just a couple of times a minute while diving.
Resting heart rate.Elephant: Larger mammals tend to have slower hearts and longer lives, and elephants are among the longest-lived.
Resting heart rate.Human: About 100,000 beats a day, or roughly 2.5 billion in a lifetime, though it speeds up with exercise.
Resting heart rate.Dog: Small dogs' hearts can beat much faster than a large dog's, so the rate depends on size.
Resting heart rate.Cat: A cat's heart rate is roughly twice a person's, and rises sharply when it is stressed at the vet.
Resting heart rate.Rabbit: Rabbits' hearts race, and the animals can die of fright, which is why they need gentle handling.
Resting heart rate.Chicken: A chicken's small heart beats about five times a second, much faster than a human's, as with other small birds.
Resting heart rate.Hamster: When hibernating, a hamster's heart rate can slow to a handful of beats per minute to save energy.
Resting heart rate.Mouse: Mice live only a couple of years, so their hearts beat about a billion times in a lifetime, similar to most mammals.
Resting heart rate.Hummingbird: It can exceed 1,200 beats a minute in flight, then plunge to a fraction of that when torpid at night.

When these women first led their countri.Sirimavo Bandaranaike: She became the world's first female prime minister, in Ceylon (now Sri Lanka), after her husband was assassinated.
When these women first led their countri.Indira Gandhi: The daughter of Nehru led India for 15 years, and she declared the Emergency in 1975, which suspended civil liberties.
When these women first led their countri.Golda Meir: Born in Kyiv, she raised her family in Milwaukee, and she once said that she had been the only man in her cabinet.
When these women first led their countri.Margaret Thatcher: Britain's first female prime minister served for 11 years and was nicknamed the 'Iron Lady' by a Soviet newspaper.
When these women first led their countri.Gro Harlem Brundtland: The Norwegian leader later chaired the commission that popularised the term sustainable development, and she led the WHO.
When these women first led their countri.Corazon Aquino: She came to power after 'People Power', following the assassination of her husband Benigno, and she helped restore democracy in the Philippines.
When these women first led their countri.Benazir Bhutto: She was the first woman to lead a Muslim-majority country, and she was educated at Harvard and Oxford.
When these women first led their countri.Angela Merkel: A physicist by training, she was raised in East Germany, and she led Germany for 16 years.
When these women first led their countri.Ellen Johnson Sirleaf: Liberia's president was the first elected female head of state in Africa, and she won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2011.
When these women first led their countri.Julia Gillard: Australia's first female prime minister came to power after her party ousted Kevin Rudd, and she was born in Wales.

Caffeine, from a sip to too much.Cup of decaf coffee: Decaf is not caffeine-free, and a cup still has small amounts, and removing caffeine is done with water or solvents.
Caffeine, from a sip to too much.Can of Coca-Cola: The first cola drink originally used extract of the kola nut, a natural source of caffeine, but now has less than coffee.
Caffeine, from a sip to too much.Can of Mountain Dew: The citrus soda has more caffeine than many colas, and its original ad slogan was 'Hillbilly drink'.
Caffeine, from a sip to too much.Single espresso shot: A single shot of espresso has less caffeine than a cup of drip coffee, as it is a smaller volume, though more concentrated.
Caffeine, from a sip to too much.Small can of Red Bull: The energy drink's caffeine comes with taurine, and one can has about the same as a cup of coffee.
Caffeine, from a sip to too much.Cup of brewed coffee: A cup of coffee has roughly this amount, and the amount depends on the roast and the brewing time, with light roast having slightly more.
Caffeine, from a sip to too much.Big can of Monster: The energy drink in a big can has a lot, and it may be more than a cup of coffee, and some people drink two a day.
Caffeine, from a sip to too much.Caffeine pill: A typical pill is about two cups of coffee, and these pills are popular with students for exams.
Caffeine, from a sip to too much.Safe daily limit (adult): Health agencies suggest adults keep to about this limit, which is about four cups of coffee.
Caffeine, from a sip to too much.Estimated lethal dose: Caffeine can be deadly in huge doses, and a person would need to drink dozens of cups of coffee in a few hours.

When these cities got their new names.New Amsterdam to New York: The English seized the Dutch colony in 1664 and renamed it for the Duke of York.
When these cities got their new names.Edo to Tokyo: Tokyo means eastern capital, and the Emperor moved there from Kyoto in 1868.
When these cities got their new names.St. Petersburg to Petrograd: It was renamed in World War I because the German-sounding burg seemed unpatriotic, then became Leningrad and was changed back.
When these cities got their new names.Christiania to Oslo: The city had been named for King Christian IV, and Oslo is the older medieval name that was restored.
When these cities got their new names.Constantinople to Istanbul: Istanbul was already the common Turkish name, but a 1930 postal law got the world to use it.
When these cities got their new names.Saigon to Ho Chi Minh City: Renamed for the revolutionary leader after reunification, though many locals still say Saigon.
When these cities got their new names.Salisbury to Harare: The old British capital was named after a prime minister, and it became Harare after Zimbabwe's independence.
When these cities got their new names.Bombay to Mumbai: It takes its name from the goddess Mumba Devi, worshipped by the original fishing communities.
When these cities got their new names.Madras to Chennai: The name comes from a Telugu chieftain's name, Chennappa Nayaka, whose father had sold land to the British.
When these cities got their new names.Calcutta to Kolkata: The spelling was changed to match Bengali pronunciation of the city's name.

Facebook through the years.Thefacebook launches: Mark Zuckerberg launched it from his Harvard dorm room, initially for Harvard students only, and it spread to other colleges within weeks.
Facebook through the years.News Feed arrives: Users protested loudly when it arrived, yet their usage rose, a pattern the company would see many times afterward.
Facebook through the years.Like button: It was nearly called the Awesome button before the team chose Like, and it later spread across the web.
Facebook through the years.Timeline profiles: This redesign turned your profile into a chronological story of your life, with a big cover photo.
Facebook through the years.Facebook IPO: It raised about $16 billion, among the biggest tech IPOs ever, and valued the company near $100 billion.
Facebook through the years.Reactions beyond Like: Love, Haha, Wow, Sad and Angry joined the thumbs-up, after tests of what people wanted to express.
Facebook through the years.Cambridge Analytica scandal: Data on up to 87 million users was harvested, and the company later paid a $5 billion fine to the FTC.
Facebook through the years.Libra coin announced: The crypto project was later renamed Diem and was shut down in 2022 after pushback from regulators.
Facebook through the years.Renamed Meta: The rebrand focused on the metaverse, and the parent company now owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp.
Facebook through the years.Threads launches: It reached 100 million sign-ups in about five days, faster than any app before it at the time.

US and architectural paper by area.Index card: Swedish botanist Linnaeus is said to have invented them for sorting plants.
US and architectural paper by area.Half Letter: It is also known as Statement, and is the size of many planners and small notebooks.
US and architectural paper by area.Executive: It is a rarely used size, once standard for executive stationery.
US and architectural paper by area.Letter: Most countries use the A4 system, so US Letter is unusual and its size is mostly a historical accident.
US and architectural paper by area.ARCH A: ARCH sizes fold in half, so ARCH A is the half-sheet of ARCH B.
US and architectural paper by area.Legal: Used for contracts and legal papers, it is longer than Letter, and the name stuck even though few lawyers use it.
US and architectural paper by area.Tabloid: Also called Ledger, it is twice the size of Letter and was named for newspapers of the same format.
US and architectural paper by area.ARCH B: It is the size of drawings, and a half of ARCH C.
US and architectural paper by area.ARCH C: Designers favour this size for posters and mid-sized drawings.
US and architectural paper by area.ARCH D: The standard size for blueprints and large posters, nearly a metre across the long side.

The Crusades, in chronological order.Urban II's call at Clermont: Pope Urban II's speech at the Council of Clermont drew the crowd's roar of Deus vult, God wills it.
The Crusades, in chronological order.Crusaders take Jerusalem: The First Crusade ended in the capture of Jerusalem, which founded the Kingdom of Jerusalem and other crusader states.
The Crusades, in chronological order.Edessa falls: The fall of this city to Zengi shocked Europe and prompted the Second Crusade.
The Crusades, in chronological order.Saladin wins at Hattin: Saladin destroyed the crusader army here and recaptured Jerusalem a few months later.
The Crusades, in chronological order.Richard arrives at Acre: Richard the Lionheart reached this port during the Third Crusade, and the city fell within weeks.
The Crusades, in chronological order.Crusaders sack Constantinople: The crusaders attacked Christian Constantinople, and Venice's famous bronze horses of St Mark's came from this plunder.
The Crusades, in chronological order.Children's Crusade: The movement of thousands of young pilgrims is legendary, and historians doubt many details of the tale.
The Crusades, in chronological order.Frederick II regains Jerusalem: He got Jerusalem back through negotiation, not battle, while excommunicated by the pope.
The Crusades, in chronological order.Louis IX captured in Egypt: The French king was captured at Mansura and was released for a huge ransom.
The Crusades, in chronological order.Fall of Acre: With this fall, the Crusaders lost their last major stronghold on the mainland of the Holy Land.

Ancient and medieval India, in order.Harappan cities flourish: Cities like Mohenjo-daro had planned streets and drainage systems, but the Harappan script remains undeciphered.
Ancient and medieval India, in order.Vedic period begins: The Vedic period produced the Vedas, among the oldest scriptures of Hinduism, passed down by memory for centuries.
Ancient and medieval India, in order.Maurya Empire founded: Chandragupta Maurya founded the empire, and at its height it covered most of the Indian subcontinent.
Ancient and medieval India, in order.Ashoka takes the throne: After the bloody conquest of Kalinga, Ashoka embraced Buddhism and nonviolence and had his edicts carved on pillars and rocks.
Ancient and medieval India, in order.Kushan Empire arises: The Kushans controlled much of the Silk Road trade, and their gold coins showed Greek, Persian and Indian deities.
Ancient and medieval India, in order.Gupta Empire founded: The Gupta era is often called India's golden age, with the mathematician Aryabhata working during it.
Ancient and medieval India, in order.Harsha's reign begins: Harsha ruled much of northern India, and the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang visited his court and wrote of it.
Ancient and medieval India, in order.Chola revival: Vijayalaya's revival began the Chola rise; later Chola kings built the Brihadisvara Temple, and their navy reached Southeast Asia.
Ancient and medieval India, in order.Delhi Sultanate founded: It was founded after Muhammad of Ghor's death by his general Qutb ud-Din Aibak, who began building the Qutb Minar.
Ancient and medieval India, in order.Vijayanagara founded: Its capital, Hampi, was a huge and wealthy city, now a UNESCO site, ruined after the empire's defeat in 1565.

British titles, from the very top down.King: Charles III became king in 2022 at age 73, the oldest person ever to accede to the British throne.
British titles, from the very top down.Prince: The title Prince of Wales is given by the monarch, not automatic; William received it in 2022.
British titles, from the very top down.Duke: Duke comes from Latin dux, leader; the Duke of Norfolk is the premier duke and hereditary Earl Marshal.
British titles, from the very top down.Marquess: The title comes from medieval marches, border lands, and a marquess is pronounced markwiss.
British titles, from the very top down.Earl: Earl is the oldest English noble title, from the Old English eorl, and an earl's wife is a countess, as there is no earless.
British titles, from the very top down.Viscount: Viscount is pronounced vye-count and means vice-count, originally a count's deputy, ranking between earl and baron.
British titles, from the very top down.Baron: The lowest rank of the peerage; the English barons forced King John to seal Magna Carta in 1215.
British titles, from the very top down.Baronet: Baronetcies were created by James I in 1611 partly to raise money, and they are hereditary but not part of the peerage.
British titles, from the very top down.Knight: Knights are addressed as Sir, and women as Dame; the title isn't hereditary and is conferred with a sword tap on the shoulder.
British titles, from the very top down.Esquire: Esquire comes from Old French for a knight's shield-bearer, and today survives as a polite style on envelopes.

When these novelty songs were released.The Chipmunk Song: Ross Bagdasarian sped up recordings of his own voice to create the squeaky trio. It topped the US charts at Christmas 1958.
Brian Hyland's song about a shy girl in a yellow polka dot bikini reached number one in the US in 1960.
When these novelty songs were released.Monster Mash: Bobby 'Boris' Pickett's dance craze song, which reached number one in the US just before Halloween 1962.
When these novelty songs were released.Disco Duck: A radio DJ in Memphis, Rick Dees, had a US number one with this quacking dance song in 1976.
When these novelty songs were released.Agadoo: Black Lace's pineapple-and-tree dance hit became a British party classic.
When these novelty songs were released.Mr Blobby: The pink, spotted TV character from Noel's House Party took the UK Christmas number one in 1993.
When these novelty songs were released.Barbie Girl: Danish group Aqua's hit led toy maker Mattel to sue. The judge dismissed the case and told both sides to 'chill'.
When these novelty songs were released.Who Let the Dogs Out: The Baha Men's smash was a cover of a song from 1998 by Trinidad's Anslem Douglas.
When these novelty songs were released.Crazy Frog's Axel F: It began as a Swedish teenager's imitation of a two-stroke engine, then was paired with the Beverly Hills Cop theme.
When these novelty songs were released.What Does the Fox Say?: The Norwegian duo Ylvis made this viral song. Real foxes sometimes make eerie sounds known as screams and gekkering.

Prehistoric animals: who lived first?.Dimetrodon: This sail-backed predator lived before the dinosaurs, and is more closely related to mammals than to reptiles.
Prehistoric animals: who lived first?.Eoraptor: One of the earliest known dinosaurs, the small, fast Eoraptor was found in Argentina and walked on two legs.
Prehistoric animals: who lived first?.Plateosaurus: A long-necked herbivore from Triassic Europe, it was among the first dinosaurs to grow large.
Prehistoric animals: who lived first?.Dilophosaurus: A crested, two-legged predator from Early Jurassic North America, it was made famous by Jurassic Park, though the real animal had no neck frill.
Prehistoric animals: who lived first?.Stegosaurus: Its back plates and spiked tail, a thagomizer, made it a tank, yet its brain was small.
Prehistoric animals: who lived first?.Iguanodon: One of the first dinosaurs ever named, in 1825, Iguanodon has a thumb spike that early scientists mistakenly put on its nose.
Prehistoric animals: who lived first?.Spinosaurus: Spinosaurus, among the largest meat-eating dinosaurs, had a sail on its back and a crocodile-like snout for catching fish.
Prehistoric animals: who lived first?.Velociraptor: Its name means 'swift thief', and it was actually turkey-sized and feathered, much smaller than the movie version.
Prehistoric animals: who lived first?.Tyrannosaurus rex: Its bite was the strongest of any land animal ever, with teeth like bananas, and it lived at the very end of the dinosaur age.
Prehistoric animals: who lived first?.Woolly mammoth: A cousin of today's elephants, it lived in the Ice Age, and the last island populations survived until about 4,000 years ago.

Stories in the Book of Genesis, in order.Creation: Genesis 1 describes creation in six days, with rest on the seventh, establishing the Sabbath.
Stories in the Book of Genesis, in order.Expulsion from Eden: Adam and Eve are cast out after eating the forbidden fruit, which the Bible never calls an apple.
Stories in the Book of Genesis, in order.Cain kills Abel: The first murder in the Bible; God marks Cain to protect him from revenge.
Stories in the Book of Genesis, in order.Noah's flood: Flood stories also appear in the older Mesopotamian Epic of Gilgamesh.
Stories in the Book of Genesis, in order.Tower of Babel: People build a tower to reach heaven, and God scatters their language, explaining why we speak so many tongues.
Stories in the Book of Genesis, in order.God calls Abram: God tells Abram to leave home for a promised land; he becomes Abraham, honoured in three faiths.
Stories in the Book of Genesis, in order.Sodom and Gomorrah destroyed: Lot's wife looks back as the cities burn and turns into a pillar of salt.
Stories in the Book of Genesis, in order.Binding of Isaac: Abraham is told to sacrifice his son but an angel stops him; Judaism calls it the Akedah.
Stories in the Book of Genesis, in order.Jacob's ladder dream: Jacob dreams of a stairway where angels climb to heaven, and wakes calling the place Bethel, 'house of God'.
Stories in the Book of Genesis, in order.Joseph sold into slavery: His jealous brothers sell him, but he rises to run Egypt's grain stores.

Units named after people: namesake's bir.Pascal: Pascal was a French mathematician and philosopher, and the unit of pressure bears his name because he studied fluids and barometers.
Units named after people: namesake's bir.Newton: Newton's laws of motion and gravity define the unit of force, and the legend of the falling apple is likely embellished.
Units named after people: namesake's bir.Watt: James Watt improved the steam engine, and he coined the term 'horsepower' to help sell it, to compare it to draught horses.
Units named after people: namesake's bir.Volt (Volta): Alessandro Volta invented the voltaic pile, the first electric battery, and Napoleon made him a count.
Units named after people: namesake's bir.Ampere (Ampère): André-Marie Ampère founded electrodynamics, and he's the one who showed that parallel wires carrying current attract or repel each other.
Units named after people: namesake's bir.Ohm: Georg Ohm's law relating voltage, current and resistance was initially ridiculed, and he spent years in obscurity before recognition.
Units named after people: namesake's bir.Joule: James Prescott Joule, a brewer by trade, showed that heat and mechanical work are linked, which helped establish the conservation of energy.
Units named after people: namesake's bir.Kelvin (Lord Kelvin): William Thomson was made Lord Kelvin, and the absolute zero scale he proposed, minus 273.15 degrees Celsius, bears his name.
Units named after people: namesake's bir.Tesla: Nikola Tesla developed the alternating current system and the Tesla coil, and the unit of magnetic flux density honors him.
Units named after people: namesake's bir.Hertz: Heinrich Hertz proved electromagnetic waves exist, which opened the way to radio, and the unit of frequency honors him.

The Voyagers' grand tour.Voyager 2 launches: Voyager 2 launched first, despite its number, because Voyager 1 was on a faster path that would reach Jupiter and Saturn sooner.
The Voyagers' grand tour.Voyager 1 launches: Voyager 1 left second but faster, and it took the first detailed close-up pictures of Jupiter and its moons.
The Voyagers' grand tour.Voyager 1 at Jupiter: Voyager 1 discovered active volcanoes on Jupiter's moon Io, the first active volcanism seen beyond Earth.
The Voyagers' grand tour.Voyager 2 at Jupiter: Voyager 2 later photographed Jupiter and found details on moons like Europa, and the data suggested an ocean below its ice.
The Voyagers' grand tour.Voyager 1 at Saturn: Voyager 1 studied Saturn's rings and Titan's thick atmosphere, then was sent out of the plane of the planets.
The Voyagers' grand tour.Voyager 2 at Saturn: Voyager 2 observed Saturn's rings in detail, and it used the planet's gravity to continue toward Uranus.
The Voyagers' grand tour.Voyager 2 at Uranus: Voyager 2 remains the only spacecraft ever to have visited Uranus, and it discovered 10 new moons.
The Voyagers' grand tour.Voyager 2 at Neptune: Voyager 2 flew past Neptune, discovering the Great Dark Spot and geysers on its moon Triton, and then left the planets behind.
The Voyagers' grand tour.Pale Blue Dot photo: At Carl Sagan's request, Voyager 1 turned around to photograph Earth as a tiny speck from about 6 billion kilometers away.
The Voyagers' grand tour.Voyager 1 reaches interstellar: Voyager 1 crossed into the space between the stars, the first human-made object to do so, and still sends data from there.

When these won the Nobel Peace Prize.Henry Dunant: The founder of the Red Cross shared the very first Peace Prize with Frédéric Passy.
When these won the Nobel Peace Prize.Theodore Roosevelt: He became the first American to win any Nobel prize, for mediating peace between Russia and Japan.
When these won the Nobel Peace Prize.Woodrow Wilson: Though honoured for his role in the League of Nations, Wilson's own country never joined the body.
When these won the Nobel Peace Prize.Ralph Bunche: The American diplomat was the first African American to win the prize, for mediating an armistice in Palestine.
At 35, he was the youngest winner to that date, honoured for non-violent resistance to racial segregation.
When these won the Nobel Peace Prize.Mother Teresa: Born in Skopje, she founded the Missionaries of Charity in Kolkata, and spent decades caring for the poor.
When these won the Nobel Peace Prize.The Dalai Lama: The Tibetan leader, named Tenzin Gyatso, has lived in exile in India since he fled Tibet in 1959.
When these won the Nobel Peace Prize.Mandela and de Klerk: They shared the prize for ending apartheid peacefully, and held South Africa's first fully democratic election in 1994.
When these won the Nobel Peace Prize.Kofi Annan: He shared it with the UN itself, and was the first UN Secretary-General from sub-Saharan Africa.
When these won the Nobel Peace Prize.Barack Obama: Awarded less than a year into his first term, the choice was a surprise, and drew debate over what he'd yet done.

Heavyweight champs of each group.Goliath birdeater (spiders): The heaviest spider has legs spanning about 30 cm and fangs of over 2 cm. It lives in South American rainforests and mostly eats worms and frogs.
Heavyweight champs of each group.Flying fox (bats): Flying foxes are huge fruit bats, with wingspans of up to about 1.7 metres. They help pollinate and spread seeds of tropical trees.
Heavyweight champs of each group.Goliath frog: The largest frog on Earth lives in the rivers of Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea. It can reach about 30 cm long.
Heavyweight champs of each group.Chinese giant salamander: This salamander can grow up to 1.8 metres, and can live for decades. It is critically endangered, having been overhunted for food.
Heavyweight champs of each group.Ostrich (birds): The tallest and heaviest living bird can't fly, but can sprint at around 70 km/h. Its eye is bigger than its brain.
Heavyweight champs of each group.Colossal squid (invertebrates): This deep-sea giant is the heaviest invertebrate known, with eyes among the largest of any animal. Its tentacles carry rotating hooks.
Heavyweight champs of each group.Saltwater croc (reptiles): The largest living reptile has the strongest bite force ever measured in an animal. It lives in estuaries from India to northern Australia.
Heavyweight champs of each group.African elephant (land): The African elephant is the biggest land animal on Earth, and a herd is led by the oldest female. Its trunk has tens of thousands of muscle bundles.
Heavyweight champs of each group.Whale shark (fish): The largest fish is a filter feeder and harmless to people. Each whale shark's spot pattern is unique.
Heavyweight champs of each group.Blue whale (mammals): The blue whale is the largest animal ever known, and its tongue alone can weigh as much as an elephant. Its call can travel hundreds of kilometres.

When these grand railway stations opened.King's Cross, London: This London terminus has a famous Harry Potter platform, 9¾. The station opened in 1852 and takes its name from a monument.
When these grand railway stations opened.Paddington, London: Isambard Kingdom Brunel designed the station's iron-and-glass roof. It's also known as the home of a bear from Peru.
When these grand railway stations opened.St Pancras, London: Its Gothic hotel looks like a cathedral, and it is now the Eurostar terminal. A giant statue, The Meeting Place, stands under the clock.
When these grand railway stations opened.Chhatrapati Shivaji, Mumbai: Formerly named Victoria Terminus, it's a UNESCO site mixing Gothic and Indian styles. Over 3 million commuters use the area daily.
When these grand railway stations opened.Gare d'Orsay, Paris: This Beaux-Arts station on the Seine was saved from demolition and became the Musée d'Orsay in 1986. It displays the Impressionists.
When these grand railway stations opened.Antwerp Central: Nicknamed the "railway cathedral," it has a huge dome and a grand stone hall. Its tracks run through on several levels.
When these grand railway stations opened.Union Station, Washington: Daniel Burnham designed this grand Beaux-Arts station, with a barrel-vaulted hall. It is one of America's most visited sites.
When these grand railway stations opened.Penn Station (original): Its demolition in 1963 outraged New Yorkers and sparked the historic preservation movement. A new Madison Square Garden stands above.
When these grand railway stations opened.Grand Central Terminal: With 44 platforms, it has more than any other station in the world. Its ceiling shows the constellations, painted back to front.
When these grand railway stations opened.Tokyo Station: Its red-brick building, by Tatsuno Kingo, faces the Imperial Palace. Heavy bombing damaged it in WWII, and it was restored in 2012.

Top speeds of famous cars.Benz Patent-Motorwagen: Karl Benz's three-wheeler is widely seen as the first practical car; Bertha Benz made the first long road trip in 1888.
Top speeds of famous cars.Ford Model T: Ford built over 15 million from 1908 to 1927, and the moving assembly line cut its price.
Top speeds of famous cars.Jaguar E-Type: Enzo Ferrari reportedly called it the most beautiful car ever made; it launched in 1961.
Top speeds of famous cars.Lamborghini Miura: The first road supercar with a transverse mid-mounted V12; Marcello Gandini styled it.
Top speeds of famous cars.Ferrari F40: The last Ferrari approved by Enzo himself and the first from the brand to pass 200 mph.
Top speeds of famous cars.Jaguar XJ220: It briefly held the production-car speed record in the early 1990s, before the McLaren F1 beat it.
Top speeds of famous cars.McLaren F1: Gordon Murray designed it with a central driving seat and a gold-foil-lined engine bay; it set the record in 1998.
Top speeds of famous cars.Bugatti Veyron 16.4: Volkswagen's 1,000 horsepower, 16-cylinder car was named after racing driver Pierre Veyron.
Top speeds of famous cars.Koenigsegg Agera RS: Koenigsegg ran this speed in 2017 on a closed Nevada highway.
Top speeds of famous cars.Bugatti Chiron (record run): A modified Chiron hit this in 2019, the first car to pass 300 mph on a track.

How long light takes to reach us from....The Moon: Light takes only about 1.3 seconds to cross the gap, so Apollo astronauts' radio messages carried a noticeable delay.
How long light takes to reach us from....The Sun: We see the Sun as it was about 8 minutes ago, so if it vanished we would not notice until then.
How long light takes to reach us from....Pluto: About 5.5 hours on average; signals from New Horizons took about that long to arrive when it flew by in 2015.
How long light takes to reach us from....Proxima Centauri: The closest star to the Sun, a small red dwarf with at least one rocky planet in its habitable zone.
How long light takes to reach us from....Sirius: Sirius is a binary star, and its faint white dwarf companion is nicknamed the Pup because of the Dog Star.
How long light takes to reach us from....The Pleiades: The Pleiades, the 'Seven Sisters', contain hundreds of young stars, and many cultures noticed this tight cluster.
How long light takes to reach us from....Orion Nebula: Visible to the naked eye as the fuzzy middle 'star' in Orion's sword, it is a stellar nursery where stars are born.
How long light takes to reach us from....Center of the Milky Way: At the center sits Sagittarius A*, a black hole with about four million times the Sun's mass.
How long light takes to reach us from....Large Magellanic Cloud: This satellite galaxy is visible from the Southern Hemisphere, and Supernova 1987A exploded there.
How long light takes to reach us from....Andromeda Galaxy: The most distant object you can see with the naked eye, and it is heading toward our own galaxy for a collision.

Disney's Snow White, in story order.Queen asks the Magic Mirror: The famous Disney line is Magic mirror on the wall, while the Grimm queen speaks to a looking-glass.
Disney's Snow White, in story order.Huntsman spares Snow White: In the Grimm tale the huntsman is ordered to bring back her lungs and liver, and returns a boar's instead.
Disney's Snow White, in story order.She flees into the forest: Snow White (1937) was the first full-length cel-animated feature, and the forest scene is one of its most frightening.
Disney's Snow White, in story order.Finds the dwarfs' cottage: The dwarfs have no names in the Grimm tale; Disney named them Doc, Grumpy, Happy, Sleepy, Bashful, Sneezy and Dopey.
Disney's Snow White, in story order.Dwarfs come home from the mine: Heigh-Ho was written for the film by Frank Churchill and Larry Morey and has been a Disney trademark tune ever since.
Disney's Snow White, in story order.Queen disguises as a hag: In the Grimm version the queen tries three times, first with a tight lace and then a poisoned comb, before the apple.
Disney's Snow White, in story order.Snow White bites the apple: In the Grimm tale the apple piece is jolted out of her throat when the coffin is bumped, not by a kiss.
Disney's Snow White, in story order.Dwarfs chase the witch: Disney's witch falls to her death in a storm, but in the Grimm tale she is made to dance in red-hot iron shoes.
Disney's Snow White, in story order.Laid in a glass coffin: The glass coffin lets the dwarfs keep looking at her; in Grimm, the prince asks to take it away.
Disney's Snow White, in story order.Love's first kiss wakes her: The film cost about 1.5 million dollars, a huge sum in 1937, and earned far more, launching Disney's feature-film era.

Back to the Future, in story order.Doc unveils the DeLorean: The DeLorean DMC-12 was built in Northern Ireland, and production lasted only a couple of years in the early 1980s.
Back to the Future, in story order.Libyans attack at the mall: An early script had the time machine as a refrigerator, but the filmmakers worried children would imitate it.
Back to the Future, in story order.Marty lands in 1955: Michael J. Fox replaced Eric Stoltz after filming had already begun.
Back to the Future, in story order.Marty is hit by a car: The car that hits Marty is driven by his future grandfather, which sets the plot in motion.
Back to the Future, in story order.Lorraine falls for Marty: Lorraine's crush on Marty creates the paradox of the film, as Lea Thompson plays her.
Back to the Future, in story order.Marty finds the young Doc: Doc says 1.21 gigawatts, and his Great Scott! is a catchphrase.
Back to the Future, in story order.George punches Biff: George's punch is the turning point of his character, played by Crispin Glover.
Back to the Future, in story order.Marty plays \"Johnny B. Goode\": Marty plays Johnny B. Goode, and Marvin Berry calls his cousin Chuck to hear it.
Back to the Future, in story order.Lightning hits the clock tower: The lightning bolt hits the clock tower at 10:04 pm, a time the film makes famous.
Back to the Future, in story order.Back to a better 1985: The sequels Back to the Future Part II and Part III followed in 1989 and 1990.

Television firsts and hits.Baird's first TV demo: The Scottish inventor transmitted flickering images in London using a spinning disc; his early test subject was a ventriloquist's dummy named Stooky Bill.
Television firsts and hits.BBC TV service begins: The BBC began the world's first regular high-definition television service from Alexandra Palace, though it shut down for the war in 1939.
Television firsts and hits.I Love Lucy debuts: It pioneered filming before a live audience with three cameras, and Lucille Ball's pregnancy was written into the show, a first for American TV.
Television firsts and hits.Apollo 11 broadcast: About 600 million people, roughly a fifth of the world, watched Neil Armstrong's grainy first steps live.
Television firsts and hits.CNN launches: Ted Turner's channel was the first 24-hour news network, and critics mocked it as Chicken Noodle News in its early years.
Television firsts and hits.MTV launches: The first video it played was The Buggles' Video Killed the Radio Star, a fitting choice for a channel built on music clips.
Television firsts and hits.The Simpsons debuts: It became America's longest-running animated series, and began as short cartoons on The Tracey Ullman Show.
Television firsts and hits.Friends debuts: By the later seasons the six leads reportedly earned about a million dollars an episode each, and streaming keeps finding it new young viewers.
Television firsts and hits.Netflix starts streaming: Netflix began as a DVD-by-mail service in 1997 and started streaming a decade later; it now counts hundreds of millions of subscribers.
Television firsts and hits.Squid Game: This Korean thriller was among Netflix's biggest launches ever, and Lee Jung-jae became the first Asian actor to win the lead drama actor Emmy for it.
